Into the Land of Paradox

The Liondance Troupe is gearing up for a new performance. Lingyang invites you out for a meal while scouting potential customers along the way. At the last stop, you learn a food stall owner has been threatened by something called the "Jingle Beast" and a gang known as "The Savages." Moved by his story and a request from the Bei siblings, you expose the gang's scheme, and in doing so, come to learn the secret Lingyang has been carrying. After the lion dance, Lingyang tells you an old legend about the "Jingle Beast"...

A team set to compete in the Jinzhou Riverside Games suffers an accident. You came only to watch, but you invite Jiyan to join you in filling the vacant spot. At the end of the race, the Gulpuffs suddenly erupt into chaos. To find the source of the anomaly, you trace it to a Sonoro Sphere upstream. After a fierce battle, you free the reverberations of Jiyan's fallen comrades from within it...

Several residents of Jinzhou City have gone missing recently. As you investigate, you cross paths with an organization known as the Séance Society, as well as Patroller Yinlin, who is investigating them too. Working in tandem, you and Yinlin set out to uncover the truth behind the group. In the end, you defeat its leader, the Dollmaker, and bring him to justice. Then Yinlin bids you farewell and departs on a new journey of her own.

Changli asks to meet you at the pavilion, and to uncover the Secret of Immortality hidden within an unfinished Weiqi game, the two of you once again venture into Mt. Firmament. Through the machinations of the Fractsidus, the adventurer Wuli, trying to save his lover Fuling, is swept into a Temporal Disruption and survives only because you arrive in time. Within the Sonoro Sphere, you witness Changli's past and recover scattered fragments of your own. After the remaining Fractsidus members are captured, Wuli and Fuling decide to keep chasing distant horizons, and you and Changli play out the final moves of the Weiqi game...

Rumor speaks of an Arcane Artist in Jinzhou whose paintings can come to life. While investigating that artist at a client's request, you meet Zhezhi, who is looking into the same matter. Together, you discover that the mysterious artist, Mingyan, already knows Zhezhi and is being forced to forge her work. Determined to bring the mastermind's crimes to light, Zhezhi confronts the Shanyun Art Exchange in open court. With your support, she wins the argument and exposes the truth...

To find the wish-granting relics from Encore's story, you, Encore, and a young listener named Ying, who holds the treasure map, set out on an adventure together. Along the way, Ying learns that she will never see her mother again, and you discover that this story was a gift Encore's mother left for her. Wanting to give the tale a happy ending, Encore gathers everyone's signature flowers and asks Verina to create the final treasure, fulfilling both her own wish and Ying's. Then you and Encore makes a pinky promise to write new stories together in the future.

A corrupted Stellar Matrix has escaped the Error Cell and may threaten the safety of the Black Shores. To track it down, you need Camellya's help. As the investigation unfolds, the past you shared with Camellya, or rather with "Lady Flora," slowly comes to light. After crossing countless junctures, the two of you find each other again, along with the core of the corrupted Stellar Matrix. You meet Camellya at Veiled Rock, where the many timelines overlap and become one the moment she offers you a flower.

An invitation draws you into the dangerous undercurrents of the Montelli family. To investigate the mysterious death of one of its members, you join forces with Carlotta once more. When the truth is finally stripped bare, it points to the sender of the invitation: Carlotta's uncle, Capollo. Carlotta evades his snare and reunites with you, and together you destroy the plan he had devised with the Order of the Deep. Before parting, Carlotta gives you a Cat's Eye gem...

To lift the spirits of the Pilgrims they rescued, Roccia decides to stage a welcome play and perform "Pegasus" with the troupe. In search of the perfect stage prop, a "star," the two of you return to the Strand, only to become trapped in a maze of fog. At its far end, you discover plushies and the "star" who are looking for their owners. You bring them back to the troupe, and the performance is a success. After the curtain falls, the plushies finally reunite with their owners, and Roccia invites you to join the troupe...

After accidentally winning a wager, you become captain of the Troupe of Fool for a day. You and Brant set off in search of lost treasure and cross paths with the greedy pirate Aldric. At the heart of the hidden treasure, Brant sticks to the plan, taking only the sea chart before slipping away with you. Aldric, however, is consumed by his own greed and meets his end. When the adventure ends, Brant tells you the tale of the chart and the Golden Captain. You become the troupe's honorary captain, and the next adventure awaits somewhere on the horizon.

Guided by a message carrying a strange frequency, you arrive in Egla Town and join Cantarella for the Night of Remembrance. When you retire to the Porto-Veno Castle to rest, past and present begin to overlap within its halls, leading you to the answer behind the festival's riddles: the Divine Trials held by the Fisalia family. With your help, Cantarella returns the girls she once saved during those trials, and the dreamy illusion of the night fades away in a veil of gentle smoke.

The Black Alley and Talos, both destroyed years ago at the hands of the Blazing Nightwalker, suddenly reappear in Ragunna. You begin investigating alongside Zani. In the course of that search, you learn that Zani herself is the Blazing Nightwalker. After a hard-fought adventure, you defeat the current Talos and rescue the residents suffering under her tyranny. Zani then tells you why she became the Nightwalker: to protect the precious, fragile peace of ordinary life. That, she says, is how heroes are born.

Futures' Tithe

[Spacetrek Collective: Classified Archive] Interview Dossier: Hiyuki Due to multifaceted considerations, we have foregone a truly comprehensive evaluation of the representative from Ashinohara—the Miko of Flaming Sakura. The majority of the intelligence gathered herein is based on her personal testimony. In the recorder's professional estimation, corroborated through subsequent cross-referencing, she appears to harbor no intention of concealing any information regarding her background. "After all, information regarding the 'Miko of Eternal Flaming Sakura' can be found in just about any Ashinohara elementary school textbook..." According to Hiyuki's own account, the source of her Forte is the "Suzu," a Legacy Talisman worn on her right wrist. Hiyuki describes the Suzu as follows: It grants the bearer the ability to perceive and utilize "future possibilities" of oneself, though it does not allow for direct communication with these "shadows of future possibility." Rebecca's ride or die gun. Just like her, this kinetic shotgun hits like a freight train and kicks like a psycho. Every shot's a gamble, and you never know where the recoil might throw you next. 

To most, the risk of using it isn't worth the reward. But for Rebecca, this beast is what built her name in the streets. She even installed a pair of oversized cyberarms just to absorb the shock of the recoil.

"Handle it carefully, unless you're looking to paint the sidewalk with your own guts."

The collar that once belonged to Rebecca's dog, Cup-Cup. She became his owner after "scooping" him up in the middle of a gig. Her reason...? Just a soft heart she'd never admit to. He was a pug. Cute. Obedient—when he chose to be. During windy nights spent on the street, he'd curl up in her arms and share the heat.
 
She doesn't say it. Doesn't need to. But whenever Cup-Cup comes up, there's a look in her eyes. Sometimes she takes out his collar and runs her fingers over it. Wondering what she could have done differently.

Pilar's golden cyberhand, one of the few things left of his.

It didn't fit her own chrome, but selling it never crossed Rebecca's mind. Nobody ever asked if they could take it. All knew the treatment they'd get: a barrel in the face and a boot out the door.

A poster advertising trips to the Moon. There was a time you couldn't walk a block in Night City without seeing a travel promotion. In these ads, it was sold as an untouched paradise. Clean, free from the rot of corporate greed. A place where everyone lived equally. Without worry, without care. But the price tag was steep. The facilities were a joke. Word spread that it was just another corporate scam. And like all of them, it faded from the conversation.

Now, dreamers dismiss it as just another corporate con. But there's still one girl standing on a rooftop, looking up, hoping that one day she might escape to the Moon.

Braindance is the most popular form of immersive media in Night City—a technology that records and replays memories and experiences. For many, it is an escape from reality; a place to sink into illusory lives that feel better than anything the real world can offer. 

For Lucy, it is a lifeline. She has a braindance of a trip to the Moon, and it is one of her most treasured possessions. Late at night, alone in her apartment, she jacks in and lets the digital reality take her far away. She savors the tranquility, imagining a future where this dream finally comes true.

The Moon Tarot Card. It symbolizes fear, the subconscious, illusions, and truths waiting to be discovered. In the illustration, one wolf howls at the distant, unreachable moon. The other waits in silence, its gaze fixed on the first.
 
The card was a gift from Misty, who gave her a tarot reading. Lucy took it with her to the Moon—one of the few pieces of Night City she brought up there. It held a strong meaning to her. Almost magical.

An action camera Lucilla used during her time in the Pioneer Association. Though her own abilities far surpass the camera's performance, she still enjoys recording through a physical lens. Particularly on lonely nights, when she silently revisits small, unguarded moments she overlooked at the time.

Lucilla loves to immerse herself in the lives of characters on screen. These old film rolls of classic movies were the one thing she could not bear to part with when she left the New Federation.
After becoming President of the Academy, she rarely found the time to watch movies. That changed the day she noticed one of her students had appeared on a movie poster.
Now, Lucilla cherishes these film rolls more than ever.

Why take time out of a busy day to put on makeup?
Once, the answer might have been to fit the image others expected of her. But now, Lucilla simply does it to please herself.
Just as she tells her students, "Never mind what others think. Become the person you imagine yourself to be."

Unlike her brother, Rebecca never planned on becoming an edgerunner. They were both raised by the notorious merc known as Papa Sunrise—their only parent. But while he spent years hammering his legacy into both of them, Rebecca never shared Pilar's stubborn hunger to inherit their father's dream.

She wanted freedom. She wanted cute things. She wanted to find her own dream in Night City... which meant she spent a lot of time butting heads with her old man.

Life doesn't wait for anyone to make up their mind. When Papa Sunrise vanished without a trace, Rebecca and Pilar's lives took a sharp turn for the worse. They found themselves sleeping in the back of a busted-up car—once their father's loyal ride on every gig, now the only inheritance they had left.

It was Wakako, the legendary fixer and long-time associate of their father, who threw them a line—or rather, a gig. She gave them a chance to prove they were worthy of Papa's legacy. But there was still a ways to go before the siblings could truly fit edgerunner-sized shoes.

Just as Papa Sunrise had always warned, Rebecca was too emotional, too unpredictable, and far too hotheaded for Night City. She nearly tanked mission after mission; instead of following simple instructions from her fixer, she always chose to follow her gut. Pilar couldn't stand it, and the two of them would tear into each other after every job. But in the end, despite all the quarreling, she still wanted to help him achieve his dream. 

It wasn't until they fell in with Maine's crew that things finally started to turn around. Rebecca and Pilar's habit of jumping down each other's throats became the crew's daily bread—often a loud, profanity-laced background track to their lives. Others would wonder why they kept hanging out if they hated each other so much.

But deep down, they really cared about each other.

Everyone who crossed paths with Rebecca came away with the same take: loose cannon, hair-trigger temper. David knew that better than anyone; he'd lost count of the messes he'd had to scrub clean after her. To an outsider, she was a different breed of edgerunner. She didn't care about the payout or the risk—as long as a job didn't cross her moral line, she'd take it. Slip into whatever role the gig demanded. One night, she was the innocent girl caught in the crossfire; the next, a bored punk looking for trouble at a bar. But she always preferred being the muscle. Point the gun. Pull the trigger. Sort out the details once the smoke cleared. Her recklessness drove her partners up the wall, but nobody ever really hated her for it. Not when she had their backs every step of the way.
 
In Night City, surviving as an edgerunner takes more than a steady nerve; you need an edge that sets you apart. Maine had his hand cannon. Dorio, her fists. Kiwi had her tech. David had his Sandevistan, sure, but it didn't make him a killer. He was still a rookie, rough around the edges. He needed to learn how to handle iron, and he needed to learn fast. Rebecca was the natural choice to show him the way. As the crew's self-appointed weapons expert, she knew her guns like the back of her hand. On the range, she was surgical; in the streets, a bullet-storm of terror. When David realized he needed that extra bit of lethality to survive, she didn't hesitate. She threw him headfirst into the deep end. Walked him through every drill. Tried cramming a lifetime of survival know-how into the kid before the city could eat him alive.

Rebecca never bothered hiding it. She had feelings for David—plain and simple. But for someone who lived her life like a live grenade, she was surprisingly disciplined when it came to him. She kept a level head. She knew she'd never be the girl he pined for. No matter what gesture, angle, or trick she pulled to show him how she felt, it was obvious his heart would never be hers. But white flags were never in her playbook. If she couldn't have him, she'd pour all that energy into keeping him alive.
 
This was a task made all the harder—and more vital—after losing half her crew. One by one, familiar faces were reduced to cold names on a mausoleum wall. Even for a girl as tough as Rebecca, who had known loss all her life, it was too much to bear. She found a corner in a dead-end alley and emptied clip after clip into the dark, screaming curses like the noise could smother the grief clawing at her insides. Why had it turned out like this? Hadn't she paid enough? She didn't have a grand dream. She didn't care about becoming a legend. All she wanted—the only thing that mattered—was not to have to watch another person she loved flatline before her eyes.
 
So when David started loading up on chrome, carrying Maine's torch as if it were his alone to bear, she couldn't stop the dread from curling in her chest. A leader of a crew? Some hotshot merc with military-grade hardware? No. To her, he was still just a kid. A cocksure gonk with dreams big enough to swallow him whole. And Rebecca wasn't about to let that happen. Not without a fight. With new chrome arms built to handle heavy recoil, she stepped up as his second-in-command. Ready to be both his sword and shield. To make sure this fool she loved didn't get himself killed.

The fear Rebecca had carried all this time finally became a reality. Even with David's freakishly high tolerance, his body couldn't keep up with the chrome he kept stacking. That, combined with the weight of the choices he had to make, sent him sliding toward the edge of cyberpsychosis. She wanted him to go easy on himself, terrified for his mental state, but David always acted fast—just like her.
 
Their last gig was highly dangerous—if not impossible. But David insisted on having his way. Rebecca was furious, but there was no turning back. Only when it was too late did she realize the truth: they'd walked into a trap. Meticulously laid. Perfectly executed. They never suspected that their own crewmate had sold them out.
 
When they learned Lucy had been captured, David went out of his way—and out of his body—to get her back. It was a suicide mission, plain and simple. The dominoes were already falling, one bad call cascading into an avalanche of disaster. There was no time to untangle the mess. No time to second-guess. Rebecca grabbed her iron, looked at that idiot who was ready to risk everything for the woman he loved, and let out a long, tired sigh.
 
"...Fine. Sign me up, choomba. Into the fire."
 
Night City would never forget that night. Their ride speeding towards Arasaka Tower, MaxTac units spraying lead at them from both sides. David burning the Sandevistan. Again. Again. Again. To carry out a plan so reckless it might as well have been a one-way ticket. Rebecca had no choice but to support him—to make sure he made it to Corpo Plaza alive. All beneath the neon glow of Night City bleeding across the skyline.
 
Despite the odds, Rebecca held onto her hope.
 
She bet it all on Lucy. One last time, she loaded her love and courage into the chamber.

After finding herself in the Somnoire, Rebecca knew immediately that she was dead. She chose only to keep quiet about it to avoid putting that weight on Lucy.
 
"Saying it would only have twisted Lucy up even more. If she started feelin' guilty or sorry for me, that'd just piss me off."
 
On the train tearing through the dream dimension, Rebecca shrugged and fed rounds into her iron, one by one. Outside the window, stars bled past—as bright and blinding as the neon that had once painted the Night City sky. She was on her way to save someone. Same old story. She was still fighting for Lucy, someone she couldn't understand but couldn't stop admiring, either. But this time, David wasn't beside her. And the girl they were going to save wasn't running away anymore.
 
She hated admitting it, but somewhere along the ride, she'd figured out why she was really here. Even if David hadn't asked, she still would've picked up her gun and gone after that pain-in-the-ass netrunner. She was part of the crew. And the crew were the chooms Rebecca cared about the most.
 
Choose her own path, make her own decisions—it's all she ever wanted. And she's gonna keep doing exactly that. No matter the risk, she will jump into fire if needed to save her friends.
 
"A flying train, a talking kitty-cat, you and Abby... Heh, this crew of ours is scary stacked."
 
"I told you, I'm not a cat, meow... And don't forget, the goal is to recover the Dream Band..."
 
"Relax, I got it memorized! We turn that chrome-dome into scrap metal, right?"
 
"You didn't catch a word, did you..."
 
Rebecca flashed a crooked grin and scratched the white cat behind the ear, shoving her hands in her pockets as she plopped down next to you. Rover.
 
"So, uh… kinda late to say sorry for dragging you into this, huh?"
 
A fist bump. That was all it took for her to know she was forgiven. Rebecca smirked, swung Guts onto her shoulder, and strolled up to the train doors.
 
"End of the line! Let's go do what we came here to do!"

Lucy keeps most of her past to herself for a reason. Few know that this mysterious netrunner was, in fact, shown the ropes by a top-secret Arasaka educational program for kids. One might say that's not the worst hand to be dealt; that a roof over your head and a full belly is more than many can hope for in Night City. But for Lucy, there was never any other path. She was brought up in this megacorp's black site—locked away and forced to train. Day after day, year after year, breaching the Blackwall, diving into the scattered depths of the Old Net. And trying to survive the rogue AIs that lurked there.
 
As a child, Lucy's worldview was built upon Arasaka's core pillar: obedience—often mistaken for loyalty. And she was not the only one taught to believe in it. A group of children took part in the program, either taken from their parents or scooped from the street. To serve the most powerful corporation on the planet—that was the dream Arasaka planted in their heads. Within that facility, they were forced to deep-dive the Old Net, running suicide gigs on repeat. None of them knew the perfect future they'd been promised was just a chimera. An elaborate fantasy spun by Arasaka handlers to serve the company's own ends. By the time Lucy figured out the truth, it was already too late.
 
The will to survive drove them to claw their way out of the prison they had long mistaken for home. They ran as fast as they could, bullets tearing through the air all around them. Gunfire and screams exploded in Lucy's ears, one after another. But she would survive. She squeezed her eyes shut, blocked everything out, and just kept running. The exit. She just had to reach the exit.
 
She woke up in some scrapyard with no memory of how she got there, and no idea if anyone else had made it out alive. She'd escaped the chase, for now, but the fear Arasaka had carved into her wasn't going anywhere. She knew they'd be hunting her. Could feel it under her skin. After that, she never stayed in one place for too long. Always moving. Always hiding.

It started with a poster: a man in a spacesuit, pointing the way to a better future. For Lucy, it was a promise of escape. And maybe, just maybe, finding a place so far away from danger that she could stay put. On countless nights, curled up with her arms wrapped around her knees, that dream took root. Planted by fear. Loneliness. A need for a place to call home.

"Maybe on the Moon, I'll finally be free?"

Cynics laughed at the idea, certain there was no corner safe from corporate dominance. To go there would be pointless; a propaganda-fuelled pipe dream. But these were the opinions of people who had never been to the Moon. So what did they know? Lucy would go there. See for herself. Someday.

Night City seemed like a good place to hide for a while. A concrete jungle. When she first arrived, she feared Arasaka's reach was too prominent, but soon she learned to haunt the corners of the city where corporations turned a blind eye. She realized that crime and violence were the true governors here. And with her skill set and caution, she was natural merc material. An edgerunner already long in the making. Her new home wasn't completely safe for her, but for the first time in years, she felt like she could survive.

Erasing every trace of her past became her new identity. To stay alive without blowing her cover, the former netrunner prodigy lived by a simple code: Stay low. Ask nothing. Tell less. Avoid Arasaka. That was her disguise. A small principle, but it was hers. Life only truly changed when Kiwi came looking for a preem netrunner to fill a slot in Maine's crew. She brought Lucy into the fold and gave her the most useful advice she'd ever get:

"Remember. Never trust a soul in Night City."

One night, Lucy took David to her place and invited him to experience a braindance of the Moon. Since she couldn't afford to travel there yet, this was the closest she could get to the real deal. Feeling the sun on her face. Jumping and floating like a feather. Serenity. Without corpos, without gangers. It was the most precious part of herself she could share.

She couldn't deny that David piqued her interest. An Arasaka Academy dropout with the reckless ambition to become an edgerunner. Wielding extremely demanding—extremely dangerous—military-grade cyberware as if it were a toy. But he was a good kid, sincere, pure at heart. Someone she felt she could possibly trust. But Lucy had spent so long keeping the world at arm's length that she didn't know how to reach out.

After David joined Maine's crew, Lucy grumbled about being saddled with babysitting duty. But despite her protests, she took him under her wing. Became his first teacher on the streets of Night City. She showed him the ropes of a merc's day-to-day, assuming he wouldn't be cut out for the life. But as she watched the boy come into his own, the knot in her chest finally started to loosen.

Her certainty about him came the day he saved her life.

A routine night turned into a bloodbath. When Pilar fell, the crew shattered into a blur of instinct and rage. Hot-headed members like Rebecca threw themselves at the killer, while Lucy took cover to strike with caution. In the chaos, David froze. Unable to move, to fight, or even save himself. But through the mayhem, he was the only one to notice Lucy being cornered. That was all the motivation he needed. In an instant, he lunged into the fray, guns blazing. To save her.

Bang.

Smoke. Silence. A turning point for both of them.

After that, Lucy led him to the rooftop—the place where she'd always gone to look at the Moon. For the first time, she didn't go alone. She brought a boy who had nothing, who promised her everything.

He told her he'd take her there. To the Moon. Someday, somehow. A promise that burned brighter and felt more real than any neon in the city below.

So how could she not love him?

Some say that tragedy is the only truth in Night City. That happiness is just fleeting smoke.

Maine and Dorio fell on a job gone sideways. David picked up the weight. Took over the crew. Maine's legacy. The life of an edgerunner. Rebecca switched to stronger cyber-arms and swore she'd never lose anyone else. Everyone moved forward.

Everyone, except Lucy.

She stepped back. Pulled away from the crew and secretly worked to protect David from the shadows, making sure Arasaka couldn't trace him. She told no one. Especially not him. She knew David would try to stop her, or worse, follow her into the fire. That was his nature. He was obsessed with protecting her. But for once, Lucy was determined to be the one holding the shield.

She was careful, but as it turned out, not careful enough. She'd underestimated Arasaka. Their fixer, Faraday, saw the opening. Found the crack in the armor. And in it, he discovered a way to exploit the love between two edgerunners to secure his ticket up the corpo ladder.

Having snatched Lucy, Faraday forced David into a desperate rescue mission as the boy teetered on the edge of cyberpsychosis. David didn't give up, not even with MaxTac hot on his heels. Rebecca and Falco—the remains of a loyal crew—threw themselves into the line of fire just to keep him moving.

The cyberskeleton did its job. David got Lucy out... only to fall into a trap set by Arasaka. A trap with Adam Smasher waiting inside.

David held Lucy close and jumped towards the Moon, which hung cold and white above the chaos. In that moment, her kiss pulled him back from the edge. Just long enough. Just enough for a final goodbye.

Rebecca and David were gone. Only Lucy and Falco survived that day. The two of them split ways after leaving Night City, and when the dust settled, it was time to move on again.
 
There was only one place she considered her destination. A too-obvious choice. A promise, never fulfilled. Did she go there to honor it, to make a dream come true, or to hide away for good? Lucy found herself on the Moon with no answers.
 
The real experience was different than the one from the braindance, and yet, the place had felt somehow familiar. For a moment, she could've sworn she saw David out of the corner of her eye. That was when the grief finally broke through. The Moon was still the same, but the boy who'd been beside her in the braindance wasn't there anymore.
 
Yet, maybe the story wasn't over.
 
"There… is a method. To let you stay."
 
On the day she left the Somnoire, Lucy stopped at the threshold of the gateway and turned to Rover. Took one last look at the silent Moon beyond.
 
"That's not what they would've wanted, is it?"

A letter lies quietly in the files box, stamped with the seal of Lucilla's mother, Kamerel. For a memory-type Resonator, diaries, notes, or other memo-keeping tools are dangerous media. They are the driftwood a drowning sailor clings to in a shipwreck. Faced with the crashing waves of memory fluctuation, you must rely on them lest you sink beneath the tide of recollection. But the moment you begin to unconsciously depend on external objects to fill the gaps in your memory, you also accept a certain risk. That someone, for instance, might tamper with your diary to rewrite who you think you are. Therefore, Lucilla, I forbid it. I forbid you to record your private matters by any means beyond your own mind. I forbid you to speak of them. I forbid you to form such a dependence. As a memory Resonator, you must become its master, the strongest, most dangerous being in your own sea of recollection. I wish for you a life without driftwood, without refuge. Without the need for me, or anyone else. And yet, as my own body began to fail, I found myself, without realizing it, keeping a diary. Two letters, one from a school in the New Federation, the other bearing Kamerel's seal. Her handwriting is so heavy that it nearly tears through the envelope. A scrap of paper carefully torn from a notebook. It bears the Spacetrek Collective's emblem. A short message is written on the back. The first time Hiyuki heard the truth of her own past, it spilled from Gyokuro's drunken lips. Hiyuki's mouth tightened. Without a word, she poured herself a glass of the bitter liquor.
 
"Hiyuki... My dear Hiyuki..." 
"You can't do this. You can't be the damn Miko of Flaming Sakura... Your life was never meant to be like this!"
 
Hiyuki's eyes narrowed. If the people of <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> saw their usually dignified and poised Miko of Flaming Sakura acting like this behind closed doors... 
 
The second hand ticked. The minute hand followed. At last, the hour hand lurched forward. By Ashinohara time, this very moment marked Hiyuki's transition into adulthood. She sighed and downed the drink in one burning gulp.
 
"You managed. You think I cannot?"
 
The liquor scorched her throat and settled like lead in her slight frame. So this was what they called the "drink of adulthood." Its taste, she decided, was hardly worth the wait. Hiyuki stood and draped a blanket over Gyokuro's muttering form. She lingered in the corner for a long moment. At last, she stepped forward, tucked the edges tight, and closed the door softly behind her.
 
The next morning, Gyokuro's fury toward the steward tasked with the Legacy Talisman's succession rang out loud enough to be heard two streets away.
 
The Suzu's power lay in "drawing upon the future." In simple terms, it meant every use exacted a toll from the bearer's remaining lifespan. In the worst case, it meant a successor who inherited the bell today might vanish into nothingness in their very first battle against a Threnodian. Because the price was so high, successors were usually chosen early. Hiyuki had stayed at Gyokuro's side for more than a decade. Even if Gyokuro refused to name her... who else could possibly be chosen?
 
The steward, unable to handle Gyokuro's temper, could only offer a strained, placating smile. "Even if not Hiyuki, surely you must name someone, Lady Miko."
 
Gyokuro fell silent for a few breaths. She sighed, cleared her throat, and prepared to resume her tirade.
 
It was Hiyuki who finally opened the door, ending the farce.
 
"For years, I have journeyed with you through Ashinohara. I know what each duty demands." 
"I have mastered every art a miko must know. The weaving of charms, the ceremonial dances—all from teachers of your own choosing."
"Only I can ensure the name of the Flaming Sakura remains untarnished, Gyokuro... No. Lady Miko."
 
Gyokuro's brow furrowed. She waved a hand dismissively. 

"You've learned it all, have you? Then don't you realize the Suzu will be the death of you?"
"I was an orphan you took in. My family lies buried beneath the snow from that Threnodian attack. I have no attachments left."
 
The room fell suffocatingly quiet. The only sound was the raspy, obsessive scrape of Gyokuro's thumb as she rubbed the bell on her wrist. She tried to speak, but in the end, no words came.

The days following Hiyuki's succession were inevitably frantic. Where once she had simply walked in Gyokuro's shadow, she now found the weight of every duty resting on her own shoulders.
 
<te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> had long suffered under the <te href=850074>Threnodian's</te> shadow, forcing the land to weave its very survival around the mikos. As the bearer of the Suzu, Hiyuki's status was as uniquely sacred as it was heavy, and her jurisdiction covered the entirety of Ashinohara. She became a nomad of necessity, racing between different places to assist the local mikos and turn the tides of battle.
 
Yet a miko was as much a living symbol as a blade. Wherever people would gather, a miko must appear to remind them why they fought. The Miko of Flaming Sakura was no exception. Hiyuki carried both burdens well. Perhaps it was because she had learned each duty at Gyokuro's side since childhood, combat and ceremony alike had long since become second nature. The only thing missing was Gyokuro's specific Flaming Sakura swordsmanship. Gyokuro had stubbornly refused to pass down the forms, even going so far as to distance herself from Hiyuki.
 
"Fine. If you will not teach me, I will learn in secret. One day, I will master it. One day."
 
But that day never came.

"The Suzu allows the bearer to draw upon the future, and a successor who inherits the Suzu today might vanish into nothingness during their very first battle with a Threnodian..."
 
Hiyuki couldn't remember the words the steward whispered when placing the Suzu in her hands. She couldn't remember the clumsy way she tied it to her wrist, mimicking a gesture she had seen so many times. She couldn't recall the weather that day, or the face of the person who handed her the small wooden box containing Gyokuro's legacy.
 
By the time the world rushed back into focus, she was sitting alone in the hollowed halls of the seat of Flaming Sakura, clutching the wish slip that had been inside the box.
 
Blood froze in her chest. A creeping frost left her fingertips numb. Inch by inch, Hiyuki dragged herself to that familiar corner of the room and curled up. She had crumpled the wish slip earlier. Now she smoothed it flat. 
 
"...I see."
"...I accept your wish."
"...There will never be another Miko of Flaming Sakura."

"Lady Hiyuki, you have served as the Miko of Flaming Sakura for a century now. If we are to renew the contract..."
"It is of no consequence."
"Then, as per our previous arrangement... for how many years shall we set the renewal?"
"Fill it as you wish."
"I did not expect you to be quite so like the previous Miko... Ahem. Very well. As you wish, Miko of Eternal Flaming Sakura."
 
The steward bowed and withdrew, closing the door with practiced reverence. Hiyuki noted that the staff accompanying him had changed three times over the decades. She shook her head, eyes narrowing as they fell upon the envelope on her desk. After a pause, she reached instead for a teacup that had long since gone cold.
 
"Just like the previous Miko... am I?"
 
How long had it actually been since she took up the title? 
Long enough that "Hiyuki" was now a fixed entry in <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>'s history books. 
Was it a long time? 
Not long enough.
 
True to the fortune lot she had inherited that year, Hiyuki had used her own strength to prove a silent vow: There will never be another Miko of Flaming Sakura. Gradually, the voices urging her to select a successor had faded. The Office of Legacy Talismans now treated its visits to the shrine as a mere formality. Even the steward, she suspected, believed a successor unnecessary. To them, Hiyuki had become the title itself.
 
Yet Hiyuki often heard a voice. It wasn't the grating, persistent lure of the Fractsidus. It was a peaceful murmur stating facts plainly in her ear.
 
"Hiyuki, you have held on for so long. But your enemy, the <te href=850074>Threnodian</te>, has a far longer lifespan. It will wait until you die, until every miko, and every successor of every miko, has passed into memory."
"Does this path of resistance truly have an end?"
 
Cold tea is always the most bitter. The over-steeped acridity clung to her tongue, making each breath feel heavy. Hiyuki tapped a finger against the envelope on the desk. Instantly, a layer of frost raced across its surface. With one more light touch, the unopened Fractsidus seal shattered into crystalline dust.
 
Hiyuki rose and called out to the child who had volunteered to help clean the shrine, reminding her to stay vigilant and watch for intruders while she was away. Her lips curled into a smile as she ruffled the girl's hair and pressed a protective charm into her small palm.
 
"Lady Miko, where are you going to help this time?"
"Honami. I will be back soon. Keep this charm with you during this time, all right?"
 
Hiyuki waved goodbye to the little girl. As she turned to leave, the bell on her wrist caught the light, shining as brilliantly as ever.

The people of <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> had long grown accustomed to the distortions wrought by the <te href=850074>Threnodian</te>. Survival was a matter of routine: seek shelter, wait for the local miko to deploy, and if the situation spiraled, wait for the recovery teams and the Miko of Flaming Sakura to arrive.
 
To Hiyuki, this felt like just another fight among thousands. She cut through the monsters with practiced efficiency, checking the integrity of the barrier as she always did. As the civilians emerged from the shelters, parents pointed her out to their children with reverent relief. "Look, that's Lady Miko of Flaming Sakura."
 
Hiyuki offered a slight nod in response. She stepped over a fallen "No Entry" sign and turned back toward the barrier to finish her sweep.
 
Focus. Strike. Sheathe... Hm?
 
The blade passed through the air as it always did. Yet something was different. Subtle, but unmistakable.
 
Hiyuki reexamined the entire barrier. Everything appeared intact, yet a lingering, visceral wrongness clung to her fingertips. She released her hilt. Flexed her wrist. Pressed her fingers together—
 
A single drop of iridescent black mire welled from her skin. It pooled in the creases of her palm before dripping to the ground, spreading silently beneath her feet. 

Hiyuki drew her blade. Frost snapped into existence around her. First, contain it. Evacuate the civilians. Then find a way to—
 
She turned, but the cry died in her throat. There was nothing before her. It was as if the air itself vanished. For one frozen moment, Hiyuki could not breathe.
 
Honami was gone.

Aside from the shattered sign at her feet and a trace of mud creeping up the hem of her dress, there was nothing left.
 
Hiyuki reached out, but her hand recoiled on its own. She gasped for breath, but there was no oxygen. It was as if the atmosphere itself had been erased from existence. She raised her blade to strike, but found no enemy to sever. Only a faint, residual frequency remained, proof that the Threnodian had acted, for a fraction of a second, with power never before recorded.
 
According to Ashinohara's records, Honami had been pulled into another dimension at that moment. Even after a desperate appeal to the <te href=851071>Spacetrek Collective</te> for their most advanced tracking technology, not a single trace could be found.
 
When the others finally led Hiyuki away, she was still mindlessly rubbing the bell on her wrist, her mind trapped in that moment of shock.

Was this silent disaster her fault?
Of course it was her fault. As the Miko of Flaming Sakura, she had failed to protect Honami.
And of course, it was not her fault. Against the power of a Threnodian, a single person didn't matter—even one who could draw a million futures to safeguard the present.
 
Hiyuki returned to the Flaming Sakura. She took the protective charm from the child at the gate, forcing a ghost of a smile. Then she walked slowly to her room and pushed open the door. There, sitting quietly on her desk, was the envelope she had destroyed.
 
"Hiyuki, oh Hiyuki... Does this path truly have an end?"

Hiyuki didn't linger on the Fractsidus's many offers. No sane person would collaborate with those who viewed human lives as mere expendable fuel.
 
Instead, she traveled across <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>, leaving behind white paper birds infused with her own frequency. She instructed the local mikos that her mind was linked to these messengers, and should any insurmountable incident occur, she would be there the moment they crushed the bird.
 
The path of resistance against the <te href=850074>Threnodians</te>... it had to have an end. It had to.
 
It was then that Hiyuki heard word that the <te href=851071>Spacetrek Collective</te> was grappling with a critical lack of safety provisions for its expeditions. She saw an opportunity and proposed a "trade." She would ensure the safety of their exploration efforts, and in exchange, the Collective would forge her a blade using the pinnacle of Solaris technology. A weapon sharp enough to cleave through a Threnodian.
 
Hiyuki joined the Spacetrek Collective as part of the Special Response Force. The unit had once been large, but casualties mounted as Aleph-1 grew more active. So Hiyuki submitted a request, proposing that henceforth, she alone would handle Threnodian containment and ensure the safety of those conducting surveys.
 
When she first arrived here, the Collective was little more than a plot of foundation in the dirt. She watched as Lahai-Roi was built, step by step, and began to grasp the true measure of human potential. The facility's construction was a miracle, perhaps the greatest engineering feat in the history of <te href=850079>Solaris</te>. Yet it came not from gods, nor from any single hero. It was built, brick by brick, by people across all Solaris who dared to dream.
 
"Lucilla."
"Hmm?"

Lucilla casually pulled a bottle of fine liquor from beneath the desk, a specialty from Ashinohara. A student hoping to pass their finals had left it at one of Hiyuki's frequent haunts, tucked under a neat note asking for the miko's blessing.
 
Hiyuki sighed, set out two glasses, and pushed one toward the restless Lucilla.
 
"The Spacetrek Collective... it was built to explore the stars beyond Solaris, was it not?"
"That's the idea."
"How fares the progress?"
"Ugh..." Lucilla drained her drink in one go. "Still a long way off. Research is hitting walls everywhere, and the higher-ups keep breathing down our necks with impossible demands."
 
Hiyuki rubbed the bell on her wrist, her eyes downcast. 

"Have any of you ever wondered... where the end of this path is?"
 
Lucilla toyed with her empty glass, then gently clinked it against Hiyuki's.
 
"There is no end, Hiyuki. Just like what you're trying to do... No end."
"But we have to keep moving forward anyway."
"Not to reach a finish line, but to take one more step alongside the people standing next to us."
 
Hiyuki remained silent for a long time. Finally, she gave a soft nod and raised her glass, drinking deeply. The liquor scorched her throat and settled like lead in her slight frame.
 
The bell on her wrist chimed—a solitary sound, but the Miko of Flaming Sakura would take her next step regardless.

To those who raised her, "Denia" was merely another asset of the Fractsidus, another pawn for the Grand Architect.

And "Denia," strictly speaking, isn't a real name at all.

In the region where she was born, people usually say "Dasvidaniya" when parting ways, meaning "until we meet again."

For human beings, a name is a parent's first gift to their children, aside from life itself. From that moment on, the child steps into the world as someone new, growing day by day, slowly adding depth and meaning to that name.

The girl chose Denia as her name because it was the only gift her family had left for her.

Even if that family only ever existed in some fleeting fever dream.

She had scoured her birth records. She even questioned if she was not something artificially constructed. But in the end, all she ever found was a blurred image of farewell in her memory.
And it's so hard to tell anything from this little piece. Whenever she brought it up with the Grand Architect, the answer was always the same: "Memories are unreliable. Let it go. It's best you don't know."

Maybe the Grand Architect had a point.

Once she had a chat with Nastasha about her friends' names, and learned of the blessings and stories they carry. Some were hopes for peace or joy. Others were wishes or dreams. All of them, in one way or another, pointed toward happiness. Yet when she asked what "Denia" meant, she received no clear answer.

It was obvious Nastasha didn't want to talk about it, so Denia stopped asking. After a year of observing and imitating humans, she had long since mastered the arts of masking and deception.
Maybe some things could never be found out.

She wasn't even sure if that hazy memory was really hers. Maybe it came from the biological original she was modeled after... Maybe it was nothing more than something the Fractsidus planted in her to keep her in line.

She had once overheard the Fractsidus researchers mention that while the human body replaces its cells and substances every few years, something always stays, to be refined time and again. That's what makes life so special.

That's especially true for those who never find their way back... Anything that manages to stick to the memories carves deep into their souls. Even just a scent. That is why some love to watch rainstorms, while others are obsessed with an unremarkable melody. Such is the human being. Always pretending to be rational, while venting all their emotions through irrational acts.

Maybe there really was a girl named Denia, once. A girl who waved goodbye to her mother.
But was that girl truly her?

Leaning against the solid, cold side of the Voidmatter Pod, bubbles and foul liquid forced their way into Denia's mouth and nose.

Drip. Drip. Drip.

Her senses dulled. Time seemed to stretch into forever.

She felt that everything that made her was being pulled apart. Her frequency splintered into countless threads. Her body dissolved into grot, swept away into the ocean. Then she rose again, a drift of mist moving across the world from one end to the other like the wind, brushing over colorless wastelands until she reached that familiar, decaying stretch of sky.

And the silent world gazed down at her, as it always had, without a word.

When the Grand Architect chose Denia as the "vessel" for Aleph-1's powers, the decision went beyond mere physical and frequency compatibility. Unlike other Resonators—people shaped by rich lives and deep emotions—Denia was empty. A hollow shell. And the one thing a hollow shell feels toward themselves and the world, more than anything, is "nothingness." A quality that perfectly aligns with Aleph-1's logic of existence.

And just as expected, Denia managed to embrace the power. For a split second in <te href=750040>Voidspace</te>, her eyes met Aleph-1's. A fleeting moment, but long enough for Voidmatter to flood her veins and organs. It granted her the power to manipulate Voidmatter particles and forged a link to Voidspace itself.

At the time, she felt only a familiar silence in the void, along with the peace that came with it.

But as the plan progressed, the Fractsidus noticed that the Resonance between Denia and the Voidborne Threnodian was rapidly declining.

The power itself remained unchanged. Something else went wrong. The vessel meant to remain hollow... wasn't. Undoubtedly, Denia failed to reach the perfection they desired.

In trying to imitate human behavior, in mimicking emotions she was never meant to feel, she had grown a fragile, aching heart.

The heart of the weak.

And with a heart like that, she could never truly become the incarnation of Aleph-1. As a result, the Fractsidus needed to fill this vessel with something strong enough to command the "void" and complete the final step in forging Aleph-1's Resonator.

Denia had always known this day would come.

Yet when that day arrived, how was she supposed to judge the life she had lived?

A puppet. A twisted monster... Or simply a single drop in an ocean that no one will ever miss.

Sometimes she would think of the time she spent at Startorch Academy. The girl in the crowd with the unexpected smile. The girl whose gentle laughter lingered in the memories of others. The lazy girl who was sometimes flustered.

Was that girl really her?

But then again, was she really not the girl?

A smile is a convenient tool. A low-cost way to narrow the distance between you and others.

Denia first met Sigrika during a group assignment. She sat in a corner of the classroom, idly twirling a strand of hair behind her ear while observing her classmates pair up.

An afternoon breeze drifted through the doorway, kneading the hums of vehicles from the parking lot with the clamor from the square. On the wall, a poster for a Fleet Snowfluff fan meeting rustled with a sharp, paper snap.

A hesitant voice suddenly found her, pulling her out of the little moment of comfort.

"Would you like to work on the assignment with me, Denia?"

Denia turned her head and saw the orange-haired girl with her hands clasped behind her back. Habitually, she tilted her head slightly, just to be sure the question was really for her, then deepened the smile on her face.

"Sure, why not?" she replied. "But why me, Sigrika?"

Sigrika explained that, while she knew Denia usually kept to herself, she noticed the joyful smile on Denia's face as she watched her classmates make a fuss.  That made Sigrika think she must be a gentle person. The kind she'd want to be friends with.

Gentle.

Denia looked up the word later. After hearing the Grand Architect's explanation, she was certain that, when applied to her, the term carried a heavy sense of irony.

If given the choice again, Denia might have refused the invitation. A great deal of trouble could have been avoided had they never met.

Yet in that moment, she simply nodded, smiled, and told Sigrika, "Okay."

Nastasha's words from a few days ago still echoed in her ears: "The truth is, it's not that most people are not afraid of death... people simply try not to think about it."

Don't think. Don't See. Don't hear. Don't wonder.

Denia discovered that inside <te href=851069>Startorch Academy</te>, something stood between the students and the concept of death, shielding them from its weight.

By day, the campus was a hive of youthful energy, where something new waited to be discovered at every turn. At night, they gazed at the star charts, watching the dreams Professor Mornye painted across the sky. This sense of happiness shrouded their senses, blinding them to the harsh realities that "it" sees.

But all dreams eventually end. "It" will arrive one day.

At the time, Nastasha had ruffled her hair and told her, "Most kids your age don't think about things like this. You're still young. You've got a whole future ahead of you. You should be more vocal and happy, like your peers, instead of curling up in the library all day, or sitting here with a librarian like me talking about such heavy things."

"Death is the ultimate question of life, Denia, but it's a bit too early for you to be solving it. First, you have to find your own path."

Denia didn't really understand what Nastasha meant by those words. All she could do was visit the library less often afterwards.

She didn't want to make Nastasha sad.

Those close to the Grand Architect have all heard that tired story one time or another.

Once upon a time, there was a fool who became a great hero by sheer accident. To save those who were suffering, {Male=he;Female=she} bore an unimaginable price, a price that was never {Male=his;Female=hers} to bear...

The Overseers had their own takes on the story's hero. Some mocked {Male=him;Female=her}, some hated {Male=him;Female=her}, and some felt sorry for {Male=him;Female=her}. Others just laughed it off or barely paid attention.

Yet the name the Grand Architect kept bringing up, the name that often worked wonders, was nothing more than a distant, vague lie to Denia.

She didn't even know if she counted as one of "those who were suffering." She only knew that whenever she mentioned that name, the Grand Architect would respond with mocking laughter—half aimed at Denia, half at themselves.

"You know, I also think {Male=he;Female=she} should be here," they'd say. "But since {Male=he;Female=she}'s not, I guess {Male=he;Female=she} isn't as all-knowing or all-powerful as you'd hope."

"Such a shame, Denia. The god you needed most doesn't seem to need you."

Except Denia never thought of {Male=him;Female=her} as a god. If anything, she pitied {Male=him;Female=her}.

If everything the Grand Architect said was true, then the one they hailed as a savior was just another prisoner in a cage, left abandoned in this world. A person who bleeds. Who grieves. Who dies.

And that was exactly why there was one thing neither the Grand Architect nor that person seemed to understand: she would have stood before the Keystone anyway. Even without the Grand Architect's order.

Because Denia couldn't find an answer.

If people who chase ideals always end up paying a heavier price, doesn't that mean the ideal itself is flawed?

After all, in places that the person cannot see, there are always those who survive by more "elegant" rules. Exploitation. Betrayal. They enjoy the world {Male=he;Female=she} has sacrificed to protect, all while mocking the ones who throw themselves into the storm.

Why does the world always show its teeth to the kind souls? Why are those who put a price on everything the ones who endure?

And if {Male=he;Female=she} could so easily let go of {Male=his;Female=her} own past, why would {Male=he;Female=she} ever give up the little happiness {Male=he;Female=she}'d fought to grasp, just to face something as absurd and horrible as Aleph-1 for everyone else's sake?

To protect them? But who would ever understand that? What would happen when that person fell?

If the <te href=851071>Spacetrek Collective</te>'s plans could already save the majority... then what was that person struggling to achieve after all?

Most of the time, the thoughts Denia kept buried under layers of masks were simple.

She just thought that between that person, this world, and herself, at least one of them had to be wrong.

Denia's consciousness kept falling, down through the endless dark.

Absorbing the final fragment of Aleph-1 into her <te href=850072>Tacet Mark</te> had pushed her physical form past its limit. The Voidmatter overwhelmed her once more, just as it had countless times before.

Her senses dulled. Time seemed to stretch into forever.

Funny how the ending mirrored the beginning. Everything fit nicely, enough to form a perfect circle.

But unlike the first time she'd found herself here, Denia realized she had somehow stopped trembling. Her breathing steadied, and the dread that once tightened her chest had vanished.

When that gaze met hers again, she slowly reached out a hand toward the hollow eye. Then, the same hand reaching for something clenched into a fist. She raised her index and middle fingers, pointed them right at the center of that pupil, like she was taking aim.

She saw it now. How laughable Aleph-1 really was.

A god born of a meaningless world naturally possesses nothing at all. Driven by the instincts of the void, it craved everything. Still, no matter how much it consumed, how much it destroyed, it remained as it was—alone in a world of eternal silence, forever thirsting, never satisfied, leaving nothing behind.

And the solid ground for her mockery? A heart of her own. The very thing that set her apart from Aleph-1.

Even if that heart was small, fragile, and nothing much in the grand stretch of time.

Yet this "meaningless" heart had allowed her to harbor expectations for tomorrow. Just like anyone else.

There would always be those willing to live for a lie. As a certain annoying friend once said: The heart defines who we are. And with it, one gains the right to choose. Much like how humans celebrate the day they were born, a day that marks their escape from the void with a fleeting memory and a transient shape. From that day on, they could feel the world. Feel joy. Reach out to others. And because of all that, they could create something the void could never.

Denia closed her eyes. She pictured her friends across the lands of <te href=850079>Solaris</te>. Sigrika, chasing birds through a sunset field. Nastasha, bent over old books in the library. And the wanderer she'd once tricked, packing up again for another long journey, somewhere far, far away.

The thought almost made her smile. She wanted to borrow that person's tone for a second and say the words with the same serious face:

"I hope they're all happy. Joyful. Free. I hope every one of their wishes comes true."

But the words caught in her throat. Too dramatic, she thought.

So she let it go. Maybe this was enough.

Not many things in this world had ever really belonged to Denia. But now, at least, she wasn't a vessel. Not a sample. Not a pawn. The void didn't own her anymore. Neither did the orders. Neither did the lies.

She just offered up the wish, quietly. From now on, she'd be right there beside them. Never leaving.

Denia had found her own path.

——

Bang.

Now that could be the sound of a good joke being cracked. The endless dark actually had an end.

Somewhere in the gloom, someone let out a soft sigh, as if they had been waiting for a long time.

Aleph-1 has been driven back, for now. But its shadow lingers. There are still complications in <te href=260004>Lahai-Roi</te>, matters unfit for researchers that require my hand. Once they are settled, I intend to return to <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> to see it for myself. Though it has already been... Well, perhaps we will meet again there.

About the Fractsidus... You remember how I can draw upon my futures with the Suzu's power? Among them was one where I became a <te href=850074>Threnodian</te> Resonator. That possibility proved I could bear its power, and marked me as a threat in the eyes of many. That is why the Fractsidus sought me out, time and again. But you need not worry. I burned that future to ash before your eyes. The line is drawn.

Tales of your exploits abound. Folk legends across countless regions, <te href=851071>Spacetrek Collective</te> reports, slander from the lips of your enemies...Yet those remain merely the evaluations of others. It was not until I met you that I understood why they depict you as they do. Had our paths crossed sooner... I wonder, might mine have taken a different turn?

There is something I wish... No, something I must confess to you. Even now, after our time together, a sour sentiment lingers within me. If I were to name it, I would call it "jealousy." I find myself imagining your power as my own, wondering if I, too, could have... Forgive me. I simply needed to exhale this poison. If my words trouble you... then I will bear whatever judgment you deem fitting.

I once wielded my blade to see it shatter. Each strike was my prayer for spring, for the snow to thaw, and... for my own release. I believed solitude was a fate I could not escape. But when I looked at you, I realized that perhaps I may yet cling to something in this fate. I am not you, and I will never become you. Our paths may have crossed but briefly, yet knowing you walk the same path as well... I no longer feel alone.

I sculpt figurines in my leisure time. It is an intricate process, demanding one's complete focus. A state I find grounding. And no matter the medium or style, there is always a reference, a clear set of steps to follow. Adhere to them, and a repeatable result is assured. Such certainty is rare to find these days.

<te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> still occupies my thoughts... but I would not call it a burden. The past is settled. What remains is to handle what was left behind. Even if it is nowhere to be found on any map, the land still carries a legacy meant to endure.

Gyokuro tea. It is <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>'s specialty. When I was young, I would steal sips from the adults' cups. All I tasted then was bitterness. But by the time I learned to appreciate the sweet aftertaste, I realized I had begun to miss that bitterness instead.

Confections, I suppose... Not from any preference of palate. It is simply that sweetness, upon tasting, stirs memories of a bitter kind. The sweeter the past I once held, the more bitter the aftertaste that lingers.

My wish is... that there will never be another Miko of Flaming Sakura. That no further fate need be bound to the <te href=850074>Threnodians</te>. Perhaps... all we have ever sought is a world where every soul is simply granted the right to live an ordinary life.

The bell I wear on my wrist is what we call a "Legacy Talisman" in <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>. For us Mikos of Flaming Sakura, it is a sacred relic passed down through generations—a vessel of Ashinohara's wishes. Through it, I gain the power to burn my futures, a power said to originate from Ashinohara's Sentinel. I know you share a close bond with the Sentinels. If you wish to see it, I can show it to you. Oh... the cord tied to the bell? Gyokuro braided it for me when I was a child. That alone is mine. The only thing that is.

If you wish to know more about my past, you will find snippets of it in the records of <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>. They tell a far more vivid tale than I ever could. After all, my only memory of the past is me striking that blade, again and again and again.

She is a bright spirit. I am aware of certain secrets she carries. In a sense, we are both bound by our pasts. But she has a future she is galloping toward, one filled with light and hope she wholly deserves. That said, I still believe she should refrain from using her Forte to slip into class when she is late.

Chisa is also from <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>. I have made a point to avoid meeting her. After all, in our homeland, Mikos only appeared in the darkest of times. We were never omens of good fortune—perhaps a parallel can be drawn to those detective comics popular nowadays. Besides, it may be unsettling to see a name from history standing before you in the flesh. Also, please do not speak to her of what transpired in Ashinohara. That burden is not hers to bear.

A resilient child. She surely endured unimaginable hardship to return here. When she vanished within the simulator cockpit, I was out on a field assignment. The investigation team later briefed me on her case. The detail that made me pause was her writing "saving the world" as her career aspiration... Hm, I find myself wondering... what in her upbringing instilled this level of conviction?

She bears an awful load for a child of her age. She seeks to shoulder the expectations placed upon a <te href=700025>Solsworn</te> far ahead her own time. I have noticed her watching the Shiratori I send forth. Perhaps I should fold one for her before I depart?

I... believe I failed her, in a way. Had I been quicker to see through the Fractsidus's plot, she might not have suffered as she did. I borrowed your strength when I delivered that strike. Only then was I able to restore a whisper of her true self back to her. I pray it caused no lasting harm. I am told that she is recovering. If we meet again, I will offer my apologies in person.

Though Lucilla insists our partnership is only contractual, I am well aware that without her discreet arrangements, I would have no place in the <te href=851071>Spacetrek Collective</te>, much less have obtained that blade. She carries herself lightly, yet the weight on her shoulders is plain to see. She often visits me, half in jest, declaring that she intends to "call it quits"—it is her way of venting. Before returning to <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te>, I should at least see her through the troubles presently at hand.

A joyous birthday to you. The day of one's birth signifies the commencement of all things. It is a guidepost to your origin and an anchor should you ever drift. I first thought to prepare a traditional gift. Yet upon reflection, there is no offering more fitting than this single, blank paper. Please, write your wish here. Hold nothing back. Whatever it may be, I shall make it come true.
(Effort sound)
(Effort sound)

I am Hiyuki, the last Miko of Flaming Sakura. Should you seek to slay the Threnodians, my blade and I stand at your service.
...Ephemeral are the blooms.
Entrust your wishes to me.
Mm, I am here.
Very well. As you wish.
Hm, I feel it now. A sharper edge now rests within my grasp.
To refine one's skill is a lifelong pursuit. Perhaps we may reach greater heights together.
With this strength, I shall safeguard more wishes.
The path I walk stretches into the future. The wishes laid upon me… perhaps one day, I can finally make them...
You hear the ring of my blade, do you not? It is the sound of my conviction to see through your wishes. Any of them.
Be gone.
Dissipate.
Rest now.
Time to end this.
Too late to escape.
You should have run.
Wait for the moment.
Is that the best you can do?
Restless already?
Nuisance.
Follow my moves, if you can.
Evanescent morning dew. Vanish!
You've prepared for this, have you not?
Your days are numbered.
No chance.
Drift with snowflakes.
Swirl.
Fall in my wake.
Down you go!
Brittle snow.
Fading bloom.
Waning moon.
Brittle snow.
Fading bloom.
Waning moon.
...Let there be snow.
A life as fleeting as the first snow.
Take your final dive, into Naraka.
May the sakura incinerate. Burn this self away.
Roam above the inferno, gazing at the snow.
For all wishes spoken, this vessel I offer.
You can trust me.
Futile.
Too slow.
Heh, it's been so long...
Worry not for me.
Be cautious. Stand back.
I cannot fall now.
Destined... to fade...
I've... seen this coming...
An ending, as it is...
Heed the summon.
Lend me your strength.
Careful. Get behind me.
An intriguing device.
There it is.
Let's get moving.
You keep it.
Anything you might need?
Our rightful claim.

What's so bad about a pretty illusion? Even an empty gift box is still nice to look at, right? Since people only believe the "truth" they want to believe, maybe the real truth isn't all that important. If the world is made of little lies to begin with, why be afraid of all the deception in our lives?

So, how've you been sleeping? I heard if you get enough rest, you wake up refreshed and happy every single day. Haha... Must be nice, I wouldn't know. But sleeping itself is nice, I think. After all, every time I drift off, it feels like a death rehearsal.
So... if falling asleep feels like a kindness, then maybe death isn't really all that scary, right?

You seem so sweet and dependable on the outside, but deep down… you're always a little guarded... What? Got fooled too many times that now it's just a reflex? Poor thing, that's got to be tiring. Well, it's not like I have anything to hide from you. So maybe, every now and then, you could try trusting me.

I used to think the world was rotten right down to its core. Like everything was hopeless. Meaningless. And I never believed any of the things the Spacetrek Collective likes to say. I mean, if life is such a gift, then why do babies cry the moment they're born? It's like they're scared, like they already know. They know it all just goes back to the Void, back to darkness. But... whenever someone holds my hand and shares their heart with me, I can feel that annoying warmth again. It feels real. It coaxes me. Tries to show me happiness might actually be real... Ha. What a joke.

Even now, I still believe the Void is unbeatable.
For most people, suffering has an end. They live their lives, close their chapters, and get their happy ending.
But you? Where does your suffering end? Not in any future that I can see, at least.
Still, if you do end up in the Void one day, don't panic... Because somewhere inside all that nothingness, I'll be there.

I'm a total sucker for those obscure lectures from sweet professors, plus anything warm and sugary... Oh, and those reference books that make zero sense. They help me pass out so much faster! You get it, right? It's impossible to get good sleep at home.
Well, the side effects aren't as bad now, but I'd give anything for Aleph-1 to just stop mumbling nonsense in my head.
A birthday cake, of course. The kind with tons of fresh fruit and way too much whipped cream. And candles on top, for sure... Why? Because I've never actually had one before.
I hate eating anything raw! Especially that fancy sliced meat on a platter.
Good sleep, good food, and... good friends together. Every single day.

People keep asking why I don't wear the uniform... Well, the whole point of the Academy uniform is its Voidmatter protection, right? But guess what the Academy has my Forte registered as? "Capable of creating bubbles that can isolate Voidmatter and offer protection." Hehe, surprise, surprise.

It was just... a lot of time in a dim room. Surgeries. Performance tests. Over and over... Nothing but bad memories, really. But I did like that little garden outside my room. True, they were just plants that grew under the Voidmatter's influence, but they had these colors... Unique and beautiful.

I find myself wondering... how nice would it be if Sigrika were just an ordinary girl?
Without all that weight on her shoulders.  They say you eventually have to pay for being innocent, but what did the kind and pure ever do to deserve that? The world can be so cruel. It punishes the kindest people and calls it "growth." Like that makes any sense.
But through it all, Siggy has never been afraid... She really is amazing.

That miko from <te href=851074>Ashinohara</te> is so powerful. Like she's cheating, you know? Yeah, I'd heard the stories before. But facing that power myself was a whole different story.
She wasn't exactly what I pictured, though. Beyond all that strength and the gentleness you can tell right from her face, there's something else, almost... clinging to her. Something that won't wash away. Loneliness... or maybe regret?
If growing stronger really comes with a price, I wonder… what has she given up to get this power?

She was one of the few Overseers in the Fractsidus who would talk to me. When I was floating in the Voidmatter pod, she'd even play the violin for me. I really enjoyed her music. It's just... I never figured out how someone who could make such beautiful melodies... would ever want to help a maniac like the Grand Architect.

Professor Mornye fits every idea I've ever had of a perfect teacher: She has a soft voice, a sweet heart, she knows her stuff inside and out, and her classes are seriously intense. And the best part? She never, ever calls on me to answer questions when I'm napping in her class! Although... it might also be that no one has ever dared to sleep in her class before.

She's the legendary Fleet Snowfluff, right? I totally recognized her back in <te href=750040>Voidspace</te>.
The Academy's former beloved star—even the toughest professors still talk about her after all these years. Plus, she still holds the top score on every single machine at the Mind Dive Arcade! Honestly, if you want your classmates to trust you, all you have to do is try to act like her... Her charm is seriously next level.
Speaking of which... you must be really proud of her, huh? Make sure you protect her well this time. Don't ever lose her again.

Seriously? You picked me to celebrate your birthday with you? But your cake does look pretty good... Mind if I steal a bite?
Haha, just kidding. This is your big day, huh? Happy birthday!
I sincerely wish that, as you journey forward, your heart stays full of happiness, and that nothing—no matter how absurd or painful—ever truly defeats you.
Better start running. Oh? You actually got away. Hmph, lucky for you.

One. Two. Three. Four… A bit off, maybe?
Fi-five! No!

Now, a volunteer from the audience...
Want me put you down? Well, since you asked nicely… Hehe.
Surprised to see me? Haha, relax. I told you we'd meet again.
Shh... Keep this between us, will you?
Fine, fine... I'll help.
Fighting alongside you? Okay, that's new.
I'm not much of a fighter... Can I just slack off?
It feels like I can control more Voidmatter now. Hmm... Getting stronger is always a good thing, right?
So you just need more power? I see... But to borrow my power? That's far too risky.
Be careful. I can feel it, Aleph-1... It never really left.

You knew the risks, and yet... you still came this far. You are just... impossible. Always. But thanks to you, I can stabilize Voidmatter now. It's a bit embarrassing to say, but... I think I want to use this power to protect everyone.

Existence is meaningless. Life is meaningless. We are meaningless. And thinking about this meaningless world is meaningless too—or so Aleph-1 says. But meaningless as I am, I can still hear my own heartbeat. I can still hear the laughter we shared... And now, I believe some things are real. Maybe that's how it's always been: I'm more afraid of being alone than I ever was of the void.
Piece by piece!
Bit by bit!
Get lost.
Burn!

Shut up.
Over here.
Surprise, surprise!
No hiding!
So annoying!
Do we have to fight?
Are we done yet?
*Yawn* I'm beat.
Meaningless fight.
I'm done being soft.
Just give up.

In you go!
Enough!

Wanna come in?
Banish!
Devour.
Take a bite?
Please don't… pity me.
Please don't… look at me.
Please don't… forgive me.
Bursting bubbles!
To silence!
Grant. Infinite. Silence.
Ashes to ashes!
Radiance no more!
Darkness. End. Permanent.
Is it my turn?
I said… don't touch them!
Hah. Tired of running?
Too slow.
Too close!
How disappointing.
Quiet!
Right back at ya!
Anything else?
Mm-hmm?
You're getting on my nerves.
Wait. That's not fair!
Need to focus…
Ugh... My head...
Let's get this over with.
I... I can still...
Everything, fading into oblivion...
The void, and the darkness…
Someone's still… waiting for me…
Now, do as I say.
Lend me your hand.
Wait, again?
Don't push your luck.
My body feels so light.
It's okay to fly sometimes, I guess.
Hiding something, are we?
My feet hurt…
Well, better than nothing.
A little pocket money.
Can I trade these for desserts?
They'd better be worth something.
Now they're mine!
Make sure no one sees it.
Oh, please…
Make it quick.

Gotta admit, Solaris ain't a bad place to live. But the peeps here are nova-level sticklers. So freakin' polite it's even got me swearin' less... Didn't know I could talk 'thout droppin' so many f*ckin' F-bombs.

Say, you ever had a dog? I did, name was Cup-Cup. Cutest little scruffball you ever saw. Knew how to listen, too. Had his own threads, a dog tag, the whole deal. Man... slept a helluva lot warmer with him around...

...Y'know, never once stepped foot in a school. Everything I know 'bout stayin' alive, I learned on the streets. Constant threat of gettin' flatlined is the best education there is—just never know how high a price you're gonna pay... But hey, even if learnin' how to survive costs a literal arm and a leg, I still call that a bargain, choom.

I can crash, like, literally anywhere. I mean, who needs a pillow when ya got hands?! Sure, fluffy bed's nice 'n' all, but once you've zonked out in a shot-up convertible on the street, you can get your beauty sleep any place, any time.

I don't bother with "right n wrong," "pros and cons"... it's too damn exhaustin'. See somethin' tasty—scarf it down. Hear someone's bullsh*t—call 'em out. Land a gig—lock 'n' load. Strike it rich—hug your crew. Life doesn't gotta be complicated.

What am I into? Do gig afterparties count? Nothing beats grabbin' a fizzy and plantin' myself on the hood of a car. My sh*thead brother clownin' around. Kiwi and Falco clinkin' glasses. Maine "mentoring" David, gettin' sloshed... Dorio tearin' him a new one. Even Lucy the loner would stick around... But I guess that's gone now.

I'm thinkin' all these Echoes are way too cool. Pickin' just one's killin' me! Can't you rig the Terminal to deploy all the Echoes you want at once? Turn a one-on-one into a full-on swarm. Now that'd be preem!
Pizza is peak. Cheap, easy and, most importantly, it's great party fuel. Perfect for sharin' while kickin' it with the crew.
Food I won't eat...? Hmm... Nope, never heard of it!
A dream? I guess... just makin' sure everyone gets to live a decent life? I dunno, choom. Too busy thinkin' about the next stunt we're gonna pull!
Ya like Guts? My own custom job. Talks the talk, packs a mean punch. Before I chromed up my arms, the recoil would send me flyin'. Total pain in the buns.

Becomin' an edgerunner wasn't my dream. Was what my pops wanted for me and my bro. Took a little while for things to click, but by the time we joined Maine's crew we'd already built ourselves a pretty savage rep... Whatever. All in the rearview now.

Lynae and I just click. Got a lot in common—graffiti, motorbikes, badass vibes... Even went racin'. I ate her dust, but whatevs. Not many students 'round here are as nova as she is. Rare breed for sure. Be cool as hell if I got to be her classmate.

Lucy... Dunno where to even start. Known her a while now, but can't say I really get her, y'know? Far as her netrunnin' skills go, she's a freakin' code wizard, can't deny that. I guess... no matter what, Lucy's crew. That answer your question?

Mornye's chrome legs and what I've got installed are toootally different. Hers are see-through! Can look right through 'em 'thout seein' a single wire or chip! Like, how's that even work? Uses 'em like she was born with 'em, like the kid's had 'em since forever—Wait, what...? She's OLDER than me?! The hell?!

At first, he gave me creepy scavenger vibes. Boy, was I wrong. Hear he's good at patchin' peeps up, even their minds. Might let him scan my skull sponge when the dust settles. See if my grayware needs tuning, or if I'm just a certified whackjob.

Sigrika's a good kid. Too good. Bein' that responsible, with everyone expectin' so much...? Gotta be exhaustin'. She oughta cut loose more. Go wild sometimes, y'know? ...Speakin' of, think she'd be down to hit the arcade with me next weekend?

It's your freakin' birthday, choom! That's a once-a-year license to raise hell! We're throwin' a rager, downin' bottles 'til sunrise! ...Oh, guess some peeps can't drink yet... Fiiiine, guess we'll make do with fizzy sodas!
Aww, where'd you come from? Who's a good baby?! Yes, you are! You're a good baby! Look how cute he is. Good boy, good boy. Aren't you cute. Buh-bye, see ya 'round!
